units.text: Amazon S three stores files in the cloud. Let’s see how S three names and retrieves a file, then look at what changes when you choose a storage class or turn on versioning.

S three is object storage. You upload data without managing storage servers. For S three Standard, 11 nines of durability is a design target for retaining data. The ninety-nine point nine nine percent availability target is about being able to access it.

A data lake might hold logs for analysis, while an app might store customer uploads. Backup and archiving are different uses, too: a backup helps you recover, while an archive keeps data you rarely need to open.

Lifecycle rules transition or expire objects. Replication makes a copy in another bucket. A notification can trigger work when an upload lands. Access controls decide who can act, while versioning keeps earlier copies of the same object.

An app uses put to upload and get to retrieve. It names the bucket and the object key. After a successful write, S three reflects the change in later reads and listings. S three Standard stores data across at least three Availability Zones.

The bucket is the container. The object is the data plus metadata, such as a content type. Its key is its full name in that bucket. A prefix groups keys with a shared beginning, and the Region tells you where the bucket lives.

Choose a Region when you create a bucket. In the shared namespace, the name must be unique within its A W S partition. The example uses lowercase words and hyphens and starts and ends with a letter or digit.

Here the key is images slash cat dot jay peg, the contents are the photo, and image slash jay peg tells an app what type of file it is. A version I D identifies one stored copy of that key. An object can be up to fifty terabytes.

This log looks nested under a date, but a general purpose bucket stores a flat list of keys. The console uses slashes to show a folder-like view. To find one day's logs, list keys that begin with that date’s prefix.

Start with the access pattern. Standard suits frequent reads, and Intelligent Tiering fits changing access. One Zone I A suits data you can recreate. For archives, Glacier Instant Retrieval gives millisecond access, while Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive require a restore. Check minimum billing durations, too.

With versioning on, uploading report dot P D F again saves a new version without replacing the earlier ones. A normal delete adds a delete marker, so a regular get no longer returns the file. You can still retrieve an earlier copy by its version I D.
